title: Video-IFBench: Can a Video Model Follow the Instruction, Not Just Watch?
hook: Video benchmarks mostly ask whether the model got the answer right. This one asks whether it did what you told it to — and more than 20 recent multimodal LLMs still struggle.
key_points: Existing video benchmarks score task accuracy, leaving instruction adherence largely unmeasured.
Video-IFBench tests constraints grounded in the video's visual and audio content, not just text formatting.
Its taxonomy has four instruction templates: single-task, multi-task, selection, and nested.
Coverage spans 32 task types and 39 hand-designed constraint categories, semantic and format alike.
A semi-automatic pipeline — MLLMs plus programmatic processing plus human verification — yields 1.5K samples at lower annotation cost.
Across 20+ recent MLLMs, failures cluster on many-constraint prompts, semantic constraints, and nested conditionals that require picking a branch from what the video shows.
content_html: Multimodal LLMs have gotten good at video understanding — but "understanding" is scored generously. Hongbo Liu and colleagues (arXiv, August 2026) point out that real requests come wrapped in constraints: answer in this form, only about this segment, and if the person on screen is holding a tool, do this instead. Existing benchmarks measure whether the answer is right, not whether those conditions were honored.
extra_html: Video-IFBench is built to score adherence. The authors define four instruction templates — single-task, multi-task, selection, and nested — spanning 32 task types and 39 manually designed constraint categories, covering both semantic requirements and output-format ones, and importantly including constraints grounded in what's visible or audible in the clip. To make that affordable, they built the 1.5K-sample set with a semi-automatic pipeline combining MLLMs, programmatic processing, and human verification. Evaluating more than 20 recent MLLMs, they find video instruction following still broadly unsolved: performance drops as constraints pile up, semantic constraints prove harder than format ones, and nested conditionals — where the model must select a branch based on what the video shows — are the sharpest failure mode. Details and per-model results at the arXiv link.

related.title: SemComp-Bench: Judge the Video by the Outcome, Not the Frames
related.hook: Most video-generation benchmarks grade appearance consistency. SemComp-Bench asks a blunter question: did the task in the prompt actually get done?

related.title: V-Rubrics: Grading a VLM's Answer Fact by Fact
related.hook: A single ungrounded object or misread chart value can sink an otherwise good answer — and a pass/fail reward can't tell you which part broke. V-Rubrics hands out partial credit per visual claim.

flashcards.prompt: What gap in existing video benchmarks does Video-IFBench target?
flashcards.back_html: They measure task accuracy — did the model understand the video — but not instruction adherence: whether it satisfied the user's stated constraints while answering.

flashcards.prompt: Which instruction types did models find hardest in Video-IFBench?

choices.text: Prompts with many constraints, semantic constraints, or nested conditionals needing a branch chosen from video content
Short single-task prompts with a strict output format

flashcards.explanation_html: Constraint count, semantic (rather than format) constraints, and complex conditional structures were the main failure modes across the 20+ MLLMs evaluated.
